newsitem.title: UK: British tabloid apologises over hoax Diana tape. [CORRECTED 11:09 GMT]
newsitem.headline: British tabloid apologises over hoax Diana tape. [CORRECTED 11:09 GMT]

text.p: Britain's Sun newspaper, in a deeply embarrassing front-page apology, admitted on Wednesday it was hoaxed with photographs it had claimed showed Princess Diana cavorting with former lover James Hewitt.
The video from which the grainy black-and-white pictures were taken was made as a pilot for a comedy show, it said.
Rivals had a field day, rubbing salt into the wounds of the Sun, which is Britain's biggest-selling daily newspaper and part of magnate Rupert Murdoch's global media empire.

The Daily Mirror devoted seven pages to the story, detailing how the video, sold to the Sun as a product of secret service snoopers peeking through the windows of palatial Highgrove Mansion, was shot for 650 pounds (less than 1,000 dollars) from the back garden of a modest south London house.
The people in the film were look-alike actors.

"We were conned by cunning fraudsters into believing that two people frolicking together on a poor quality film were the Princess of Wales and her former lover James Hewitt," the newspaper's editor Stuart Higgins announced.
"The Sun apologises profusely to both of them for any hurt or offence caused," said the newspaper which has often led the tabloid frenzy surrounding the royal family.
He called it "one of the most elaborate hoaxes of the decade".

Diana, 35, reacted calmly to the rumpus, saying in a short statement she did not recognise herself or former cavalry officer Hewitt in the video, which was shown again and again by a Murdoch satellite television company on Tuesday.
Hewitt, who served in the Gulf War, said he would be consulting his lawyers, opening the prospect of a potentially-costly court case for the Sun.

In 1987 the Sun was forced into a humiliating climbdown when pop singer Elton John won a million pounds ($1.5 million) in libel damages after the newspaper published untrue allegations about his sex life.
The Sun had claimed the so-called "spy video" had confirmed Diana's fears that she had been under surveillance during the collapse of her 15-year marriage to heir to the throne Charles.
Diana has admitted she "adored" Hewitt during a five-year affair before her separation from Charles in 1992.
Amateur film-maker Nick Hedges told the Daily Mirror, the Sun's chief competitor, that he made the video in the hope it would help him and the two actors to win some comedy work.
"Never in a million years would I have thought this would have been taken seriously," he said, adding he planned to sue for breach of copyright, ownership and confidentiality.
Notorious hoaxer Rocky Ryan, who has fed a stream of fake stories to the tabloids over the years, said British newspapers would publish almost anything about the royal family.
"It would be a piece of cake to flog a story like this," he told the Guardian broadsheet newspaper.

Higgins's crushed pride will take time to recover but his mortification pales compared to that of the Sunday Times which in early 1983 published what it thought were the secret diaries of German dictator Adolf Hitler (corrects by removing reference to Andrew Neil who was not the editor of the Sunday Times at the time).

The diaries were in fact the work of German antique dealer Konrad Kujau, who hastily produced 60 fake tomes before bashing the covers with a hammer and sprinkling used tea leaves over the pages to convince the Murdoch-owned Sunday Times of their authenticity.

In the 1970s the Daily Express triumphantly announced that Martin Bormann, the senior Hitler aide believed to have died in the last days of World War Two, was living in South America. Sadly for the paper, "Bormann" turned out to be a schoolteacher.
